output.title: Testimonial consent is not the final check
output.body:
If a customer story ever gets used, consent is only one part of the check. The harder question is whether the wording still matches what was actually done, and whether it starts implying results or capabilities that were not shown.

That matters for a small business because a quote can drift into a promise. Someone may agree to be quoted, but that does not automatically mean they approved every channel, every edit, or every implied conclusion. It also does not turn a pilot into proof of scale. A pilot is still a pilot. It is not evidence of ROI or a finished system unless those points are explicitly supported.

The practical next step is simple: before anything is published, write down three things in plain English — what was actually done, what the person agreed could be said, and what claims are off limits. Then check the draft against those three notes. If it reads like a guarantee, it needs another pass. Human approval should stay in the loop before anything goes public.
